Bidisha: Vinita, what's the plan for this weekend?
Vinita: Revising all of chemistry. Saturday and Sunday. Done by Sunday night.
Bidisha: That's what you said about physics.
Vinita: This time it'll work. Physics had the visit to my aunt's.
Bidisha: How far did you get with physics?
Vinita: Half the chapters.
Bidisha: And biology before that?
Vinita: Also half. But chemistry is lighter.
Bidisha: Is it? There are fourteen chapters. The test is on Tuesday.
Vinita: I'll start at eight and go straight through. A weekend is enough.
Bidisha: You've said a weekend is enough three times now.
Vinita: It only failed because of things that happened.

qa.q: How many chapters does chemistry have?
What does Vinita feel about the new weekend plan?
qa.a: Vinita feels confident it will work this time, and seems defensive about the earlier plans that stopped at half.

qa.q: What could Vinita try in place of one weekend for a whole subject?
qa.a: Vinita could look at how much was done last time and spread chemistry over several evenings, since half a subject is what a weekend has given before.

qa.q: How does Bidisha see the plan?
qa.a: Bidisha notices that physics and biology both stopped at half and that Vinita has said a weekend is enough three times, so worries the plan will fail again.

grounding: A teenager plans a whole subject's revision in one weekend, misses each time, and repeats the same plan for the next subject.

subtype: Approach: repeats the same underestimate again and again [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Jyoti, and in Class 10 I had a special talent: making the same plan fail again and again. In October I said, "This weekend, I'll finish all of biology." By Sunday night I'd done two chapters out of twelve. So I made a new plan: "Next weekend, all of chemistry." Same thing: three chapters. My brother Santosh watched me write "All of physics!!" on my whiteboard for the third weekend. "Didi, how many chapters did you finish last time?" "Three." "And how many are in physics?" "Fourteen." He raised his eyebrows. I rubbed out the board, embarrassed. I'd never once looked at how much I actually got done before planning the next weekend.

qa.q: How many chapters of biology did Jyoti finish that weekend?
How did Jyoti feel when Santosh asked his questions?
qa.a: Jyoti felt embarrassed, seeing clearly for the first time that the weekend plans never matched reality.

qa.q: What would you advise Jyoti for the next plan?
qa.a: Use how many chapters she really managed, about two or three, to plan, and spread each subject over several weekends.

qa.q: How does Santosh see his didi's whiteboard plans?
qa.a: Santosh sees the pattern clearly and seems gently amused, using simple questions instead of teasing.

grounding: A teenager keeps planning to revise a whole subject in one weekend, misses each time, and repeats the same plan for the next subject.

passage:
Class teacher's note: Francis, Class 11, before the midterms

Francis came to me on Monday, worried he was behind. He showed me his revision planner. Every weekend in the last month had the same kind of entry: "Sat–Sun: complete Economics." "Sat–Sun: complete Accountancy." "Sat–Sun: complete English." Next to each, in smaller writing, "not done." When I asked how much he usually finishes in a weekend, he said, "Maybe three chapters." Economics has eleven. Yet the next page already said, "Sat–Sun: complete Business Studies." His classmate Noor, who sits next to him, said he'd been working hard but kept feeling like a failure. I sat with him and we planned one subject across three weekends, based on three chapters each.

qa.q: What did Francis usually finish in a weekend?
How had Francis been feeling about his revision?
qa.a: He felt worried and like a failure, because every weekend plan ended with "not done".

qa.q: What made the new plan more realistic?
qa.a: It used what Francis actually finishes, about three chapters, and spread one subject across three weekends.

qa.q: How might Noor see Francis's struggle?
qa.a: Noor seems concerned and fair, noticing he works hard but keeps feeling like a failure.

grounding: A teacher notes a teenager repeatedly planning a whole subject in one weekend, missing each time, and planning the same again.
